paragraphs.text: Late-onset Pompe disease, which includes juvenile and adult forms of glycogen storage disease type II, is caused by a partial deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase. Its course is more insidious than that of classic infantile Pompe disease. The typical symptoms are slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness and respiratory difficulties (Forsha et al., 2011). Weakness mainly affects the trunk, proximal lower limbs, and respiratory muscles, and onset can range from the first year of life to the sixth decade (Herbert et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: Makos et al. (1987) reported 3 sons of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. Each developed progressive proximal muscle weakness secondary to alpha-glucosidase deficiency, and each developed a fusiform basilar artery aneurysm. The aneurysm ruptured fatally in 2 of the brothers and was complicated by cerebellar infarction in the third. In the surviving brother, similar glycogen deposition was found in the smooth muscle of the superficial temporal artery.

paragraphs.text: Herbert et al. (2019) reviewed 84 patients with late-onset Pompe disease carrying the c.-32-13T-G variant. Four patients (2 males and 2 females, all Caucasian) had been diagnosed clinically and had symptom onset in the first 2 years of life. Age at onset ranged from 10 days to 20 months, and age at diagnosis from 10 to 26 months. Initial symptoms included delayed gross motor milestones, signs of proximal muscle weakness, swallowing and feeding difficulties, and sleep apnea. All 4 patients showed early, characteristic alterations in posture and movement. Despite enzyme replacement therapy, musculoskeletal involvement progressed and residual muscle weakness was evident in all of them, with ptosis, myopathic facies, scoliosis, lumbar lordosis, scapular winging, and weakness of the trunk and lower limbs. Progressive scoliosis occurred in 2 of the 4 patients. Other features included elevated CK, AST, and ALT; hypernasal voice; Gowers sign; myotonic discharges on EMG; and gastrointestinal and genitourinary symptoms. ECG and echocardiography were normal.

agent.process_note: I opened all 45 files. Only 2 were full text: Forsha et al. (2011) and Herbert et al. (2019). I read both in full and checked the variant names, ages and counts in Herbert with Grep. Ten papers were title only, and the rest were abstracts. Title-only papers are cited only for what their titles say. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the GAA MIM number and chromosomal location are left out of the intro. Herbert et al. (2019) did not give the protein change for c.118C>T in the text. Davis et al. (1976) (diaphragm paralysis with alveolar hypoventilation) and Molho et al. (1987) (twins with bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis) do not mention acid maltase deficiency in their abstracts, so they are not cited. Angelini et al. (1972) is title only (fibroblast abnormalities in adult acid maltase deficiency) and was also not cited. Byrne et al. (1986) concerns a dominantly inherited disorder with normal acid maltase and is cited only as a differential diagnosis.
